why_how.text: Many crashes with pedestrians and other vehicles happen where a driver should have come to a full stop and did not.
Steady and flashing red lights look alike but call for different actions.

scenario.text: Sara reaches an intersection where the traffic light is flashing red and no other cars are in sight.

reasoning.text: A flashing red light is treated exactly like a stop sign, so you stop and then go when the way is clear.

result.text: Sara comes to a complete stop, checks for traffic and pedestrians, and then continues.

claim.text: Common mistake: rolling slowly through a stop sign when no one seems to be coming.

correction.text: You must stop completely at a stop sign, before the stop line or crosswalk, and then yield before going.

memory_support.text: Stop at the line, stop at red, flashing red is a stop sign, stop for anyone crossing.

prompt.text: You are leaving a parking ramp and a sidewalk runs across the exit. Where must you stop?

answer.text: Before crossing the sidewalk, and again before entering the road.

rationale.text: You stop completely before entering a road from an alley, driveway, lot or ramp, and always before crossing a sidewalk or crosswalk.

narration.text: Sharing the road begins with knowing when you must come to a complete stop. This unit gathers the situations the manual lists: stop signs, entries from alleys, driveways, parking lots and ramps, red traffic signals, flashing red lights, crosswalks where someone is crossing, and a handful of special cases such as ramp meters, railroad crossings with stop signs, flag persons and raised bridges. In each case a rolling stop is not enough. You will also see how a steady red light differs from a flashing red one, which is one of the most common points of confusion for new drivers.

lines.text: Stop before the line or crosswalk
Blocked view: ready to stop again

narration.text: At a stop sign you must stop completely, before the stop line if one is marked, or before the crosswalk if there is one. After stopping, yield to pedestrians, bicyclists and traffic before you go, and if your view of the intersection is blocked, be ready to stop again for traffic or people in your path. A stop sign does not give you a turn just because you stopped first. It gives you a chance to look and to let anyone with the right-of-way go ahead. Only when the way is clear do you move through the intersection. Make the stop complete every time.

lines.text: Stop before the sidewalk or crosswalk

narration.text: You must stop completely before pulling onto a road from an alley, a private driveway, a parking lot or a parking ramp, and you must always stop before driving across a sidewalk or crosswalk. That often means two stops: one before the sidewalk, where people may be walking, and another at the edge of the road, where you look for traffic. Pedestrians on a sidewalk do not expect a car to roll across their path without stopping, so the first stop protects them. The second stop gives you time to judge gaps in traffic before you pull out.

lines.text: Flashing red: like a stop sign

narration.text: At a red traffic signal, stop and wait until the light is green and your path is clear before going. Treat a flashing red traffic light exactly like a stop sign. Stop at any crosswalk, marked or unmarked, where a pedestrian or bicyclist is crossing, and stay stopped until they have passed your lane. Full stops are also required for a red freeway ramp meter, for a railroad crossing posted with a stop sign, when a flag person or traffic device signals you to halt, and at a bridge raised for boats. Each one means stop completely before you continue.

lines.text: Steady red: stay stopped until green
Flashing red: stop, then go when clear

narration.text: Here is the classic trap. A steady red signal means stop and wait for green. A flashing red light means stop and then go when the way is clear, just as you would at a stop sign. Some drivers treat a flashing red as a slow-down signal and roll through, which is wrong, because a full stop is required. Others sit at a flashing red waiting for a green that may never come, which wastes time and confuses drivers behind them. Remember it this way: steady red waits for green, flashing red is a stop sign. Getting this pair right is one of the easiest points to earn.

Here is a quick check: you are leaving a parking ramp, and a sidewalk runs across the exit before the street. Where must you stop? Recall the entry rule. You must stop completely before pulling onto a road from an alley, a private driveway, a parking lot or a parking ramp, and you must always stop before driving across a sidewalk or crosswalk. So you stop before crossing the sidewalk, checking for people walking, and then stop again at the edge of the road before entering traffic. Two short stops keep both pedestrians and other drivers safe.

lines.text: Stop signs, red lights, flashing red
Ramp meters, rail stop signs, bridges

narration.text: To recap, stop completely at stop signs, before the line or crosswalk, then yield to pedestrians, bicyclists and traffic. Stop before entering a road from an alley, driveway, lot or ramp, and always before crossing a sidewalk. At a steady red light, wait for green; at a flashing red light, stop and go when clear, as at a stop sign. Stop at any crosswalk where a pedestrian or bicyclist is crossing, and stay stopped until they pass your lane. Also stop for red ramp meters, railroad crossings with stop signs, flag persons and raised bridges.

why_how.text: School bus rules protect children at the moment they are most at risk, getting on and off the bus.
The warning distances and the divided roadway exception are the details most often tested.

scenario.text: On an undivided four-lane road, a school bus coming toward Ben stops and turns on its flashing red lights.

reasoning.text: Without a divider, the duty to stop covers traffic from both directions, and you stop at least twenty feet from the bus.

result.text: Ben stops at least twenty feet away and waits until the red lights stop flashing.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking drivers facing a stopped school bus never need to stop.

correction.text: On an undivided road, drivers facing the bus stop too; only a divided roadway frees drivers on the far side.

memory_support.text: Yellow means slow and get ready, red means stop twenty feet back until it ends.

prompt.text: A school bus is about to stop in a fifty-five mph zone. How far ahead of the stop should its yellow lights come on?

rationale.text: In zones above thirty-five the warning lights come on three hundred feet ahead; in slower zones, one hundred feet.

narration.text: School buses carry the most protected passengers on the road, and Minnesota's rules around them are strict. This unit explains how a school bus warns that it is about to stop, the distances its yellow lights give you in slow and fast zones, why you must never pass a bus on the right while its lights flash, how far back to stop when the red lights flash, how long you stay stopped, the divided roadway exception, and the penalties for both drivers and vehicle owners. Expect these rules on your test, and expect to use them every school day once you drive.

lines.text: Thirty-five or less: one hundred feet

narration.text: A school bus warns that it is about to stop with yellow and red lights that flash in turn. In a speed zone of thirty-five miles per hour or less, the bus driver turns on the flashing yellow lights at least one hundred feet before the bus stops. In a speed zone above thirty-five, the yellow lights come on at least three hundred feet before the stop. Passing a school bus on its right side while it shows flashing red or yellow lights is against the law. When you see yellow lights flashing, slow down and get ready to stop, because red lights are coming.

lines.text: Stop at least twenty feet away
Front or back of the bus

narration.text: When a stopped school bus has its red lights flashing, you must stop at least twenty feet away from it. Whether you are facing the front or the back of the bus, you stay stopped until its red lights stop flashing. Do not start moving when the stop arm folds or when the children seem to be clear. The signal to go is the red lights turning off. That twenty-foot gap gives children room to cross in front of or behind the bus, and the rule about staying stopped keeps you from creeping forward while children are still moving.

Here is the trap. On a divided roadway, you do not have to stop for a school bus with flashing red lights that is on the other side of the divider. But that exception depends entirely on the divider. Without a divider, the duty to stop covers traffic from both directions, behind the bus and facing it. A wide road with four lanes and only painted lines is still undivided, so oncoming drivers must stop. When a question describes a school bus across the road from you, ask first whether a physical divider separates you. If not, you stop.

lines.text: At least five hundred dollar fine

narration.text: Failing to stop for a school bus is a misdemeanor, and a conviction brings a fine of at least five hundred dollars and the loss of your driving privileges. An officer with probable cause to believe you illegally passed a stopped school bus may arrest you within four hours of the violation, so the case does not end when you drive away. When you sign a driver's license application, you certify that you understand the duty to stop for a school bus and know the penalties for breaking that law, so no driver can claim not to have known.

The law also reaches the vehicle's owner. The owner or lessee of a vehicle used to break the school bus stopping law is guilty of a petty misdemeanor unless they can prove someone else was driving, in which case the driver is charged. So the driver faces a misdemeanor, while the owner faces a petty misdemeanor unless they show another person was at the wheel. If you lend your car, make sure the person driving it knows the school bus rules, because the owner can be held responsible when the driver cannot be identified.

Here is a quick check: a school bus is about to stop on a road with a speed zone of fifty-five miles per hour. How far ahead of the stop should its yellow warning lights come on? Recall the two warning distances. In a speed zone of thirty-five or less, the yellow lights come on at least one hundred feet before the stop. In a zone above thirty-five, they come on at least three hundred feet before. Fifty-five is above thirty-five, so the answer is at least three hundred feet. Use that warning time to slow down, because the red lights and the stop are coming.

lines.text: Yellow: one hundred or three hundred feet
Red: stop twenty feet back until off
Only a divider frees the far side

narration.text: To sum up, a school bus warns with flashing yellow lights at least one hundred feet before stopping in zones of thirty-five or less and three hundred feet in faster zones, and you may never pass it on the right while its lights flash. When the red lights flash, stop at least twenty feet away and stay stopped until they stop flashing, whether you face the front or back. Only a divided roadway frees drivers on the far side. Failing to stop is a misdemeanor with a fine of at least five hundred dollars and loss of privileges, and owners face a petty misdemeanor.

why_how.text: Yielding the right-of-way correctly is based on courtesy and common sense, and getting it wrong is a leading cause of crashes.
Children crossing near schools need every driver's full attention.

scenario.text: At a T intersection with no signs, Mia is turning left from the road that ends while another car approaches on the cross road.

reasoning.text: At an uncontrolled T intersection, the driver who is turning yields to all cross traffic.

result.text: Mia waits for the cross traffic to pass before making her turn.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a green left-turn arrow means you never need to yield.

correction.text: Even with a green arrow, you yield to vehicles or pedestrians already in the intersection before turning.

memory_support.text: Left yields to right, turners yield at a T, arrows still yield, processions go first.

prompt.text: A funeral procession with headlights on approaches your intersection. What must you do?

answer.text: Yield to every vehicle in the procession.

rationale.text: Once a procession marks itself with headlights or hazard warning lights, you yield to the whole procession.

narration.text: Right-of-way and yielding laws rest on courtesy and common sense, and breaking them is a leading cause of traffic crashes. This unit starts with the people who direct traffic near schools, safety patrols, crossing guards and school bus flaggers, and then turns to the yielding rules at intersections without signals, at all-way stops, for left turns and green arrows, and at T intersections. It finishes with yielding to buses merging back into traffic, funeral processions, and pedestrians and traffic when you come out of a driveway. Learn the pattern and most questions answer themselves.

lines.text: Stop for patrols and crossing guards
Wait for the bus flagger's signal

narration.text: Come to a complete stop for a student safety patrol helping classmates cross, and for an adult crossing guard holding a stop sign or flag. Driving through a line of children crossing the road is illegal even with no safety patrol present; it is a misdemeanor, and a second violation within a year is a gross misdemeanor. Stop for a school bus flagger who is holding traffic so buses can leave school property, and do not move on until the flagger or a police officer tells you to. Near schools, assume children may appear and drive ready to stop.

lines.text: Arrive together: left yields to right

narration.text: At an intersection without signals, and at an all-way stop or flashing red light, when two drivers arrive together the driver on the left yields to the driver on the right. When turning left, yield to oncoming vehicles that are in the intersection or near enough to cause a crash. A green left-turn arrow still requires you to yield to vehicles or pedestrians already in the intersection before you continue in the arrow's direction. These three rules cover most intersection questions. When in doubt, the driver who would cross another driver's path is usually the one who waits.

lines.text: Turning driver yields at a T

narration.text: Here is a trap built on the rule you just learned. At most uncontrolled intersections, when two drivers arrive together, the driver on the left yields to the driver on the right. But an uncontrolled T intersection follows its own rule: the driver who is turning yields to all cross traffic. That means the driver on the road that ends must wait, even if the cross traffic is coming from the left. When a question shows a T, do not apply the left-right rule. Ask who is turning off the ending road, and that driver yields.

lines.text: Yield to a marked funeral procession

narration.text: A driver in the right-hand lane yields to transit and metro mobility buses merging out of a bus stop or off the shoulder, and to a school bus re-entering the lane after loading, which shows its left turn signal. Yield to every vehicle in a funeral procession once it marks itself with headlights or hazard warning lights. Coming out of a private road or driveway onto a public road, stop and yield to pedestrians and traffic, and at intersections and crosswalks, marked or unmarked, always yield to crossing pedestrians. These everyday yields keep traffic moving smoothly and safely.

Here is a quick check: a funeral procession with its headlights on is approaching the intersection where you are waiting. What must you do? Recall the rule. Once a funeral procession identifies itself with headlights or hazard warning lights, you must yield to every vehicle in it, not just the first one. So you wait until the entire procession has passed before you go, even if your light turns green or you reached the intersection first. Cutting into the middle of a marked procession is exactly what the yielding rule is meant to prevent, so let the whole line go by.

lines.text: Left yields right; turners yield at a T

narration.text: To wrap up, stop completely for student safety patrols, crossing guards with a stop sign or flag, and school bus flaggers, and never drive through children crossing. When two drivers arrive together at an uncontrolled or all-way intersection, the left yields to the right, but at a T the turning driver yields to all cross traffic. Left turners yield to oncoming traffic, and a green arrow still yields to anyone already in the intersection. Yield to merging transit and school buses, to marked funeral processions, and to pedestrians and traffic when leaving a driveway.

why_how.text: Emergency crews need a clear path and safe space to work, and the rules for approaching and stopped emergency vehicles are different.
Two short rules about fire vehicles are easy to forget.

scenario.text: On a highway with two lanes in his direction, Omar sees a tow truck stopped on the shoulder with its flashing lights on.

reasoning.text: Under the Move Over Law, tow trucks count as emergency vehicles, so you move to the lane farthest from it if it is safe.

result.text: Omar checks his mirror and moves to the left lane, passing the tow truck with a lane of space.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking the Move Over Law covers only police cars and ambulances.

correction.text: It also covers tow trucks, stalled or disabled vehicles, and stopped service, maintenance, utility, construction, postal and waste vehicles with warning lights on.

memory_support.text: Approaching: pull right and stop; stopped: move over or slow; fire trucks: five hundred back.

prompt.text: An ambulance with siren and lights approaches on the other side of a concrete median. Must you stop?

answer.text: No; a physical barrier such as a median strip separates it from your lane.

rationale.text: You need not stop for an emergency vehicle separated from your lane by a fence, wall or median strip.

narration.text: Emergency vehicles depend on other drivers to reach a scene quickly and to keep their crews safe once they arrive. This unit covers what to do when an emergency vehicle approaches with lights and a siren or bell, the barrier exception, the arrest window for failing to yield, the Move Over Law for stopped emergency vehicles and the many other vehicles it covers, what to do when you cannot move over, how far back to stay from a firefighting vehicle, fire hoses, and the basics of a safe following distance. The approaching and stopped cases have different rules, so keep them separate.

lines.text: Two-way road: move right and stop

narration.text: When an emergency vehicle with flashing red lights and a siren or bell comes toward you on a two-way road, move right and stop. On a one-way road, move to the closer side. If you are in an intersection, finish crossing it first. Then stay stopped until every emergency vehicle has gone by, because others may follow. You need not stop for an emergency vehicle that is separated from your lane by a physical barrier such as a fence, wall or median strip. An officer with probable cause to believe you failed to yield may arrest you within four hours of the violation.

lines.text: Two lanes your way: move over
One lane or cannot move: slow down

narration.text: Under the Move Over Law, when an emergency vehicle with flashing lights is stopped on or beside a road with two lanes in your direction, move to the lane farthest from it if it is safe; tow trucks count as emergency vehicles. If you cannot move over a lane, or the road has only one lane in your direction, slow down and pass the stopped vehicle with caution. The rule also applies to stalled or disabled vehicles and to stopped service patrol, road maintenance, utility, construction, postal, and solid waste or recycling vehicles with warning lights on.

Here is a trap. Many drivers think the Move Over Law is only about police cars, fire trucks and ambulances. In fact tow trucks count as emergency vehicles under it, and the same rule applies to stalled or disabled vehicles and to stopped service patrol, road maintenance, utility, construction, postal, and solid waste or recycling vehicles with their warning lights on. So whenever you see any of these stopped with warning lights, plan to move a lane away if you have two lanes in your direction, or slow down and pass with caution if you cannot.

lines.text: Five hundred feet behind a fire run

narration.text: Only vehicles on official emergency business may follow within five hundred feet of a firefighting vehicle on an emergency run. Never drive over an unprotected fire hose unless a law enforcement officer or fire department official tells you to. More generally, keep enough distance behind the vehicle ahead to stop or turn away from a collision, adjust that distance for weather, traffic and road conditions, and use the three-second rule taught later in the manual. Following too closely leaves you no room to react if the vehicle ahead suddenly stops for an emergency.

Here is a quick check: an ambulance with its siren and lights on is coming toward you on the other side of a concrete median strip. Must you pull over and stop? Remember the exception. You must move right and stop for an approaching emergency vehicle, but you need not stop for one that is separated from your lane by a physical barrier such as a fence, wall or median strip. A concrete median is such a barrier, so you may continue with care. If there were no barrier, only a painted line, you would have to move right and stop until it passed.

To finish, when an emergency vehicle with lights and a siren approaches on a two-way road, move right and stop, on a one-way road move to the nearest side, clear an intersection first, and stay stopped until all have passed, unless a physical barrier separates you. Failing to yield can bring arrest within four hours. For a stopped emergency vehicle, tow truck, disabled vehicle or service vehicle with warning lights, move a lane away when you can, or slow down and pass with caution. Stay five hundred feet behind fire vehicles on a run, never drive over a fire hose, and keep a safe following distance.

why_how.text: Being pulled over is stressful, and knowing what to do makes the stop safe for you and the officer.
Careless and reckless driving are crimes, not just bad habits.

scenario.text: Lena sees police lights behind her at night on a two-lane road near a bridge.

reasoning.text: When emergency lights appear behind you, stay calm, slow down, signal and pull onto the right shoulder as soon as it is safe, avoiding bridges, curves and the traffic lane.

result.text: Lena signals, waits until she is past the bridge, pulls onto the shoulder, turns on her interior light and keeps her hands on the wheel.

claim.text: Common mistake: reaching for your license as soon as the officer walks up.

correction.text: Tell the officer where your documents are before reaching, and keep your hands visible on the wheel.

memory_support.text: Calm, signal, shoulder; light on, hands on the wheel, tell before you reach.

prompt.text: You have a firearm in the vehicle when an officer approaches. What should you do?

answer.text: Keep both hands on the wheel, tell the officer about the firearm and where it is, and never reach for it.

rationale.text: Telling the officer right away with your hands visible keeps the stop calm and safe.

narration.text: This unit covers two connected topics. First, it defines careless and reckless driving, two offenses that are tried in court. Second, it walks through what to do and expect when a law enforcement officer pulls you over: how and where to stop, what to do after dark, how to handle your documents, what to do if you have a firearm in the vehicle, how to respond if you disagree with a citation, and why obeying lawful orders matters. The manual's goal is a stop that is safe for everyone, and a few simple habits go a long way toward that.

Careless driving means driving or stopping a vehicle in a way that endangers people or property. Reckless driving goes further: it means knowingly ignoring a substantial and unjustifiable risk to others, and it includes racing whether or not the speed limit is exceeded. In other words, racing another car is reckless driving even if both drivers stay at or under the limit. A charge of either careless or reckless driving is tried in court as a misdemeanor. The difference between the two is about awareness: reckless drivers know the risk and take it anyway.

When emergency lights appear behind you, stay calm, slow down, signal and pull onto the right shoulder as soon as it is safe, avoiding bridges, curves and the traffic lane. On a multi-lane road, if you are nearer the left shoulder and it has room for a full lane, you may pull over onto the left shoulder instead of the right. Signaling shows the officer you have seen them and are looking for a safe spot. Do not stop on a bridge or a curve just because the lights came on there; drive on carefully to the first safe place.

During a stop after dark, switch on the interior light, keep the doors shut, stay inside unless the officer says otherwise, and keep your hands visible on the steering wheel. If your license or insurance proof is out of reach, tell the officer where it is before reaching, and do not get out of the vehicle or approach the officer unless you ask and are given permission. These habits let the officer see what is happening inside the vehicle and understand your movements before you make them, which keeps the encounter calm and predictable for both of you.

Here is a situation where the order of steps matters. With a firearm in the vehicle, leave both hands visible on the wheel, tell the officer about the firearm and its location as soon as they approach, and never reach for it. The trap is reaching for your documents, or worse, toward the firearm, before you have said anything. Speak first, keep your hands still, and follow the officer's instructions about what to do next. Being clear and early about the firearm is the single most important step in keeping that stop safe.

If you disagree with a citation, do not argue at the roadside; explain your view in court, and ask any questions before the officer finishes the stop. Not obeying a lawful order or direction from an officer is illegal and can lead to arrest, and you should not resist if taken into custody. Traffic enforcement aims to change unsafe behavior, reduce crashes and injuries and save lives, and a warning or citation is meant to deter future unsafe driving. Seen that way, a stop is a chance to correct a habit, and arguing at the roadside helps no one.

Here is a quick check: you have a firearm in your vehicle, and an officer is walking up to your window. What should you do? Recall the steps. Keep both hands visible on the steering wheel, tell the officer about the firearm and where it is located as soon as they approach, and never reach for it. Then follow the officer's directions. After dark you would also have the interior light on, and as always you would stay inside with the doors shut unless told otherwise. Speaking first, with your hands still, is what keeps this stop safe.

lines.text: Pull over safely, light on, hands up

narration.text: To sum up, careless driving endangers people or property, reckless driving knowingly ignores serious risk and includes racing, and both are tried as misdemeanors. When lights appear behind you, stay calm, signal and pull onto the right shoulder when safe, or the left shoulder on a multi-lane road if it is closer and wide enough. After dark turn on the interior light, keep doors shut, stay inside and keep hands on the wheel. Tell the officer before reaching for documents and about any firearm right away, argue a citation in court, and obey lawful orders.

why_how.text: Knowing what a citation means and what fleeing costs helps you respond calmly to any stop.

scenario.text: After a stop, Jay is handed a citation and worries that signing it means admitting he broke the law.

reasoning.text: Accepting a citation is not an admission of guilt; it only acknowledges receipt and promises to appear in court if required.

result.text: Jay accepts the citation and plans to explain his side at the hearing.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking fleeing police is only a traffic ticket if no one is hurt.

correction.text: Fleeing a police officer in a motor vehicle is a felony, punishable by up to three years and one day in prison, a fine of up to five thousand dollars, or both.

memory_support.text: Accepting is not admitting; fleeing is a felony that grows with harm.

prompt.text: Which forms of identification are accepted at a traffic stop?

answer.text: A Minnesota or out-of-state license, temporary license, learner's permit, military ID, or consulate or international license.

rationale.text: The officer will usually ask for your license and proof of insurance and check that the license is valid.

narration.text: This unit picks up where the traffic stop left off. You will learn what an officer usually does during a stop, which forms of identification are accepted, what accepting a citation does and does not mean, where citations go and the options a court may offer, how to raise concerns about an officer's conduct, and the penalties for fleeing police, which rise sharply when someone is hurt or killed. Understanding the process makes a stop less stressful and helps you see why staying put and handling disagreements in court is always the right choice.

While every traffic stop varies, during a stop the officer will usually greet you, say they are a law enforcement officer, ask for your license and insurance proof, explain the reason for the stop and check that your license is valid. Identification accepted at a traffic stop includes a Minnesota or out-of-state driver's license, a temporary license, a learner's permit, a military ID, and a consulate or international driver's license. Having your documents ready and telling the officer where they are before you reach makes this part of the stop quick and smooth for everyone involved.

Accepting a citation is not an admission of guilt; it only acknowledges that you received it and promises that you will appear in court if required. Citations go to a local jurisdiction for a hearing, and the court may offer a diversion program such as driver education training. Concerns about an officer's conduct go to the officer's agency or supervisor, using the officer information printed on the citation. So you have clear, lawful ways to dispute a citation and to raise a concern about the stop, and none of them involve arguing at the roadside.

lines.text: Up to three years and one day

narration.text: Some people imagine that driving away from a stop is a minor offense. It is not. Fleeing a police officer in a motor vehicle is a felony punishable by up to three years and one day in prison, a fine of up to five thousand dollars, or both. That is far more serious than the citation the stop might have produced. Whatever the reason for the stop, and even if you disagree with it, the lawful choice is to pull over safely and handle the matter through the citation and hearing process you just learned about. Pulling over safely is always the lawful choice.

lines.text: Great bodily harm: up to seven
Substantial bodily harm: up to five

narration.text: The penalties grow when fleeing hurts someone. If someone dies because a driver fled police, the penalty reaches up to ten years in prison and a twenty thousand dollar fine. Great bodily harm brings up to seven years and fourteen thousand dollars. Substantial bodily harm brings up to five years and ten thousand dollars. Those numbers show how seriously Minnesota treats the danger a fleeing driver creates for everyone else on the road. The penalties climb with each level of harm, so the stakes of fleeing are enormous.

Here is a quick check: an officer asks for identification during a stop. Which forms are accepted? Recall the list. Accepted identification includes a Minnesota or out-of-state driver's license, a temporary license, a learner's permit, a military ID, and a consulate or international driver's license. The officer will usually also ask for proof of insurance and check that your license is valid. If any of these documents are out of reach, tell the officer where they are before you reach for them. Having them organized in one place makes the stop faster.

lines.text: Accepting a citation is not guilt

narration.text: To wrap up, during a stop the officer usually greets you, identifies themselves, asks for your license and insurance, explains the stop and checks your license, and accepted identification includes licenses, permits, military IDs and international licenses. Accepting a citation is not admitting guilt, citations go to a local hearing where diversion may be offered, and conduct concerns go to the officer's agency or supervisor. Fleeing police is a felony with up to three years and one day, rising to ten years and twenty thousand dollars if someone dies.

why_how.text: Pedestrians have no protection in a crash, so drivers carry most of the duty to keep them safe.
Pedestrians have their own rules, which help drivers predict what they will do.

scenario.text: The car in the lane next to Nora stops at an intersection, though her own light is green and she sees no reason for the stop.

reasoning.text: Passing a vehicle that has stopped for a pedestrian is illegal, so when another vehicle stops, look for someone in the crosswalk and be ready to stop.

result.text: Nora slows, spots a pedestrian stepping out ahead of the stopped car, and stops.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a crosswalk only counts if it has painted lines.

correction.text: An unmarked crosswalk is where a sidewalk meets the road with no lines painted, and pedestrians there have the same protection.

memory_support.text: Lines or no lines it is a crosswalk; never pass a car that has stopped.

prompt.text: Where should a pedestrian walk when there is no sidewalk and walking on the road is necessary?

answer.text: On the left side, facing oncoming traffic.

rationale.text: Where there is no crosswalk, a pedestrian yields to all vehicles and walks facing traffic if on the road.

narration.text: Pedestrians can appear anywhere: on busy city streets, in small towns and along highways. This unit covers the duties drivers have toward people on foot: never passing a vehicle stopped for a pedestrian, taking special care with blind pedestrians, knowing what marked and unmarked crosswalks look like, the penalties for breaking pedestrian right-of-way laws, and the places where extra caution is needed. It also explains the rules pedestrians themselves follow, which helps you predict their movements. Walking and driving rules fit together, and both sides do better when they know them.

lines.text: Passing a car stopped for a pedestrian is illegal

narration.text: Passing a vehicle that has stopped for a pedestrian is illegal, so when another vehicle stops, look for someone in the crosswalk and be ready to stop. The stopped vehicle may block your view of the person it stopped for. Breaking pedestrian right-of-way laws is a misdemeanor, and a second violation within a year becomes a gross misdemeanor. So treat any vehicle stopped at a crosswalk as a warning sign. Slow down, look around it, and stop if a pedestrian is crossing, even if your own light is green. Slow down early whenever you see a car stopped ahead.

lines.text: Quiet near canes and guide dogs

narration.text: A marked crosswalk has solid white lines and may have signs or flashing lights, while an unmarked crosswalk is where a sidewalk meets the road with no lines painted. Both are crosswalks. Watch for blind pedestrians carrying a white or metallic cane or using a guide dog, and do not honk or rev the engine near them. When you stop at any crosswalk, do not block it with your vehicle. Watch extra carefully for pedestrians on streets lined with parked cars, in poor visibility and wherever children are around, because those are places people step out unexpectedly.

lines.text: No paint does not mean no crosswalk

narration.text: Here is a trap. Some drivers think that without painted lines there is no crosswalk, so pedestrians there are crossing at their own risk. The manual says otherwise. An unmarked crosswalk is the area where a sidewalk meets the road with no lines painted, and the yielding rules apply there just as they do at a marked crosswalk. When you approach a corner where sidewalks meet the street, expect people to cross. Treat the corner as a crosswalk, be ready to stop for anyone crossing, and do not stop with your vehicle blocking the path.

lines.text: Obey signals; wait back from the road
No crosswalk: yield and face traffic

narration.text: Pedestrians should obey signals, wait a few feet back from the road for the WALK signal, still yield to vehicles already in the intersection, and make eye contact so drivers yield before they cross. Where there is no crosswalk, a pedestrian yields to all vehicles, and if walking on the road is necessary, walks on the left side facing oncoming traffic. At night or in poor visibility, pedestrians should wear light-colored clothing with reflective material or carry a flashlight, and expect that sun glare may keep drivers from seeing them. Drivers should watch for people doing exactly this.

Here is a quick check: there is no sidewalk, and a pedestrian has to walk along the road. Where should they walk? Recall the pedestrian rules. Where there is no crosswalk, a pedestrian yields to all vehicles, and if walking on the road is necessary, they walk on the left side facing oncoming traffic. That way the walker can see the vehicles coming toward them. At night they should also wear light-colored clothing with reflective material or carry a flashlight. As a driver, expect walkers on the left side of rural roads and give them room.

lines.text: Never pass a car stopped at a crosswalk
Walkers face traffic, wear reflective gear

narration.text: To finish, never pass a vehicle that has stopped for a pedestrian; look for someone crossing and be ready to stop. Breaking pedestrian right-of-way laws is a misdemeanor, and a repeat within a year is a gross misdemeanor. Marked crosswalks have white lines, and unmarked ones are where a sidewalk meets the road. Stay quiet near blind pedestrians, watch carefully near parked cars, in poor visibility and around children, and never block a crosswalk. Pedestrians wait back for the WALK signal, make eye contact, walk facing traffic where there is no sidewalk, and wear reflective clothing at night.

why_how.text: Bicycles are legal vehicles, so drivers and riders share the same lanes and many of the same rules.
The three-foot passing rule is the most tested bicycle item.

scenario.text: On a narrow two-lane road marked as a no passing zone, Ali comes up behind a bicyclist riding near the right edge, with no oncoming traffic in sight.

reasoning.text: You may cross the center of the road to pass a bicyclist even in a no passing zone when it is safe, leaving at least three feet between your car and the rider.

result.text: Ali checks that the rider is not signaling a left turn, crosses the center line and passes with more than three feet of space.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a driver may use a bicycle lane whenever no bicyclist is in it.

correction.text: Driving in a bicycle lane is illegal except to park where allowed, to enter or leave the road, or to prepare for a turn.

memory_support.text: Bikes are vehicles; three feet to pass; bike lanes only to park, enter, leave or turn.

prompt.text: How does a bicyclist signal that they are stopping?

answer.text: By holding the left arm bent down toward the ground.

rationale.text: A right turn is shown with the left arm bent upward or the right arm held straight out.

narration.text: Bicycles are legal vehicles on Minnesota roads with the same rights and responsibilities as other vehicles. This unit covers how drivers should share the road with them, including bicycle lanes, turning across a bike lane, the minimum passing distance and the special permission to cross the center line to pass. It then turns to the rules bicyclists themselves follow: obeying traffic laws, riding with traffic, signaling, stop signs, lane position, riding side by side, lights and sidewalks. Knowing the rider's rules helps you predict what a bicyclist will do next.

lines.text: Only to park, enter or leave, or turn

narration.text: Driving in a bicycle lane is illegal except to park where allowed, to enter or leave the road, or to prepare for a turn, and you must yield to approaching bicyclists before moving into it. Before turning across a bicycle lane, make sure it is clear, signal, and move into the bicycle lane before you make the turn. Moving into the lane before turning means you do not cut across a rider who is coming up on your right. Always yield to approaching bicyclists before you move into the lane. Moving in early also signals your plan to riders behind you.

lines.text: At least three feet of space
May cross center in a no passing zone
Make sure the rider is not turning left

narration.text: When passing a bicyclist, leave at least three feet between the side of your car and the rider. When it is safe, you may cross the center of the road to pass a bicyclist even in a no passing zone, after making sure the rider is not signaling or turning left. That special permission exists so that drivers can give riders the full three feet instead of squeezing past. Take your time. Wait behind the rider until oncoming traffic clears, then pass with plenty of room, and return to your lane only when you are well clear of the bicycle.

Here is a distinction that trips people up. Electric-assist bicycles have an electric motor that helps with pedaling, and they follow the same road rules as bicycles. Mopeds, which have a gas engine, are not bicycles under these rules and follow different ones. So a rider on an electric-assist bicycle is treated like any other bicyclist, with the same rights to the road and the same duties. When a question mentions a motor, check what kind of motor it is. An electric assist means bicycle rules apply; a gas engine means a moped with its own rules.

lines.text: Obey traffic laws, ride with traffic
Stop signs: slow enough to stop

narration.text: Bicyclists must obey all traffic laws, ride with the flow of traffic, signal every turn and obey traffic control signs, signals and devices. At a stop sign, a bicyclist must slow enough to be able to stop before the intersection or crosswalk, and may continue without stopping when no vehicle is nearby. Bicyclists ride just to the right of faster traffic but may move toward the center of the lane for hazards, when passing or when turning left. As a driver, expect a rider to move left for these reasons, and give them the room they need.

lines.text: Right turn: left arm up or right arm out
Two abreast in one lane; lights at night

narration.text: A bicyclist signals a right turn with the left arm bent upward or the right arm held straight out, and signals stopping with the left arm bent down toward the ground. Two bicyclists may ride side by side if they stay within one lane and do not impede traffic, and riders should wear helmets for safety. At night a bicycle needs legal lights and reflectors and may use a white flashing front lamp, a red flashing rear lamp or both, and tires with spikes are allowed for traction. Recognizing these signals helps you react correctly when a rider ahead raises an arm.

Here is a quick check: how does a bicyclist signal that they are stopping? Recall the bicycle hand signals. A bicyclist signals stopping by holding the left arm bent down toward the ground. A right turn is shown with the left arm bent upward or with the right arm held straight out. When you see a rider ahead with the left arm bent down, expect them to slow and stop, and give them space. Bicyclists must signal every turn, so watching their arms tells you a lot about what they will do next. Watching a rider's arms is a simple way to stay one step ahead.

lines.text: Three feet to pass; bike lane limits

narration.text: To wrap up, bicycles are legal vehicles with the same rights and responsibilities as other vehicles. Drive in a bike lane only to park where allowed, enter or leave the road, or prepare a turn, and yield to riders first. Leave at least three feet when passing, and you may cross the center line to do so when safe. Electric-assist bicycles follow bicycle rules, while gas mopeds do not. Bicyclists obey traffic laws, ride with traffic, signal turns, slow at stop signs, ride right of faster traffic, may ride two abreast in one lane, use lights at night and yield to pedestrians on sidewalks.
